title: Fixed groups for torus automorphisms of smooth connected affine groups
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme]. An $S$-group scheme has multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams; a homomorphism respects them. A group of multiplicative type of finite presentation is an fppf-local form of $D(M)=\operatorname{Spec}\mathcal O_S[M]$ for a finitely generated abelian group $M$, with $e_m\mapsto e_m\otimes e_m$ as comultiplication [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Fppf means faithfully flat and locally of finite presentation [def-pc-fppf-site]. A torus is an fppf-local form of $\mathbf G_m^r$ for a finite integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(U)=\Gamma(U,\mathcal O_U)^\times$. A smooth affine group of finite presentation with connected geometric fibres is reductive if each geometric fibre has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent closed subgroup; unipotent means admitting a faithful matrix representation by unipotent matrices. Let $H\to S$ be a smooth affine group of finite presentation with connected geometric fibres [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions] [def-weil-connected-scheme], and let a torus $R$ act on $H$ by $S$-group automorphisms. Define $H^R(U)$ to consist of $h\in H(U)$ fixed by every $r\in R(V)$ for every $U$-scheme $V$. Then $H^R$ is represented by a smooth affine closed subgroup of finite presentation with connected geometric fibres. Its formation commutes with arbitrary base change. If $H$ is reductive, then $H^R$ is reductive. The torus need not be embedded in $H$, and the action may be trivial.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.4 and Example 2.2.6, printed pp.65--67 (semidirect-product interpretation); torus centralizers of reductive groups, paragraph before Remark 3.1.5, printed p.83; Corollary 3.3.5 proof, printed p.101 (the reductive semidirect product and its torus centralizer). WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf.

proof.text: First work over an affine base $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ where $R=\mathbf G_m^r$. Form $E=H\rtimes R$, whose underlying scheme is $H\times_U R$, with $(h,t)(h',t')=(h\,a(t,h'),tt')$ and inverse $(a(t^{-1},h^{-1}),t^{-1})$. The action identities prove the group diagrams. The subgroup $j:R\to E$ is $t\mapsto(1,t)$. It is closed: on affine coordinates its ideal is generated by $b-e_H^*(b)$ for generators $b$ of the coordinate algebra of $H$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $E$ is affine. By [lem-weil-pbc-lfp-affine-opens-finite-presentation], write the coordinate algebra of $H$ with finitely many generators and relations. Adjoining $z_i,w_i$ and relations $z_iw_i-1$ presents the algebra of $E$, so $E$ is finitely presented. It is smooth by [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]: it is locally finitely presented, and in a square-zero lifting problem the $H$-coordinate lifts by smoothness of $H$, while each unit coordinate of $R$ lifts to a unit (a lift of an inverse has product $1+$ a square-zero element). Thus all hypotheses of the relative split-torus centralizer theorem hold.

source.place: Example 2.2.6, pp.66--67: explicit semidirect-product construction over a split affine base.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer] to $j:R\hookrightarrow E$. Its centralizer $C$ is smooth affine of finite presentation, closed in $E$, and commutes with every base change. On every test scheme, $(h,t)(1,u)=(h,tu)$ whereas $(1,u)(h,t)=(a(u,h),ut)$. Since $R$ is commutative, $(h,t)$ centralizes $R$ exactly when $h$ is fixed by the full $R$-action after every further test-scheme extension. Let $F=C\times_{R}U$ using the projection to $R$ and its identity section. Then $F$ represents $H^R$, is closed in $H$, and the maps $(h,t)\mapsto((h,1),t)$ and $((h,1),t)\mapsto(h,t)$ give inverse scheme isomorphisms $C\simeq F\times_U R$. The group law on $C$ becomes the direct-product law because $R$ acts trivially on $F$.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.4 and Example 2.2.6, pp.64--67: the centralizer calculation.

proof.text: The affine coordinate algebra $B$ of $C$ is finitely presented over $A$ by [lem-weil-pbc-lfp-affine-opens-finite-presentation]. The algebra of $F$ is $B/(z_1-1,\ldots,z_r-1)$, so [lem-weil-pbc-finite-presentation-quotient-fg-ideal] makes $F$ finitely presented. It is smooth directly from [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]: for any square-zero affine lifting problem into $F$, compose with $F\hookrightarrow C$, lift using the smoothness of $C$, and then compose with the morphism $C\simeq F\times R\to F$. This composite restricts to the original point because the projection is a retraction. Thus no invalid inference of smoothness from a closed immersion is used.

source.place: Example 2.2.6, p.67: smoothness of the direct factor, with explicit lifting argument.

proof.text: These local representing functors have canonical compatible identifications on all overlaps, even for different splittings. The fixed condition is fpqc local on a test scheme: a section of $H$ glues uniquely by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent]; after any $V\to W$ and $u\in R(V)$, pull back the covering by [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change]. The two sections $a(u,h_V)$ and $h_V$ agree on that cover, hence agree on $V$ by the uniqueness assertion of the same descent node. Conversely any fixed section restricts to fixed sections. Therefore the fixed subfunctor of $H$ is an fpqc sheaf, and its locally represented identifications satisfy the cocycle condition literally, by equality of subfunctors of $H$.

source.place: Example 2.2.6 relative interpretation; fpqc subcanonicality, Stacks 023Q and 022D.

proof.text: For a general affine $U\subset S$, take an fppf splitting cover of $R_U$ and refine it by finitely many affine opens using [lem-pc-fppf-affine-refinement]. Their disjoint union $U'\to U$ is a singleton fpqc cover: its source is affine by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence](4), it is flat and surjective by the definition of the fppf cover, and it satisfies the fpqc covering condition by [lem-trf-fppf-covering-is-fpqc]. The disjoint union $F'\to U'$ of the groups constructed in steps 1--3 is affine and has its canonical descent datum from step 4. The finite coproducts used here exist by [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-coproduct-family]. Apply [lem-galois-fpqc-affine-descent-effective] to obtain $F_U$. Descend its map to $H_U$ by [lem-galois-fpqc-morphisms-descend]. Step 4 identifies its represented functor with $H_U^{R_U}$.

source.place: Relative extension of Example 2.2.6; Stacks 021P, 022B, 0245 (lemma-affine), and 0241/02W0.

proof.text: The map $F_U\to H_U$ is a closed immersion by [lem-pc-fpqc-descend-closed-immersion], using the pulled-back fpqc cover of $H_U$ from [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change]. Affineness descends by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-affine], and local finite presentation by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-locally-finite-presentation]. An affine morphism is quasi-compact and quasi-separated by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence], so $F_U\to U$ is of finite presentation. Smoothness descends by [lem-trf-smooth-fpqc-base-descent]: the finite disjoint union $U'$ of affine schemes is affine, its map to affine $U$ is quasi-compact, flat and surjective. The affine groups $F_U$ on affine opens of $S$ have canonical overlap isomorphisms since they represent the same functor. These are gluing data; [lem-weil-pbc-glue-schemes] gives a global $F$ representing $H^R$. Its map to $H$ is a closed immersion by [lem-pc-fpqc-descend-closed-immersion] for the Zariski cover of $H$. Affineness and local finite presentation follow from the same descent nodes for the Zariski cover of $S$. Smoothness follows from [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-restrict-open-subschemes](b) and [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-local-on-source]. Thus $F$ is smooth affine of finite presentation over $S$.

Fixed points form a subgroup on every test scheme: $a(u,hh')=a(u,h)a(u,h')=hh'$ and $a(u,h^{-1})=a(u,h)^{-1}=h^{-1}$, and the identity is fixed. These natural operations give the group operations on $F$ by its representing property; their group identities follow from those on $H$. For any $S'\to S$ and any $S'$-scheme $W$, being fixed in $H_{S'}(W)$ by $R_{S'}$ after every $W$-scheme extension is exactly the original condition for $H(W)$ and $R$. Consequently $F\times_S S'$ represents $(H_{S'})^{R_{S'}}$, canonically and compatibly with its inclusion in $H_{S'}$. This proves arbitrary base change, including nonflat and nonreduced base changes.

source.place: Functorial centralizer definition, Definition 2.2.1, p.64; elementary calculation with the action.

proof.text: It remains to check the geometric fibres. Fix a geometric point with algebraically closed field $k$. An fppf splitting cover for $R_k$ has a nonempty affine finite-type open over $k$; a closed point of it is $k$-rational by [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing](1). Pulling the splitting back to this point gives $R_k\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. The torus is smooth by the unit-lifting calculation of step 1. It is geometrically connected: after any field extension its coordinate ring is a Laurent polynomial domain, so its spectrum is irreducible (two nonempty basic opens intersect because the product of two nonzero elements is nonzero). Apply [lem-weil-pbc-geometrically-connected-product-components] with $X=R_k$ and $Y=H_k$. Since $H_k$ is connected by hypothesis, $E_k=H_k\times R_k$ is connected. Its identity is a $k$-point, so [lem-sbc-connected-rational-point-geometrically-connected] makes it geometrically connected. It is smooth by step 1.

source.place: Example 2.2.6, pp.66--67: passage to an algebraically closed geometric fibre; Stacks 04KV.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected] to the smooth geometrically connected affine $k$-group $E_k$ and its embedded torus $R_k$. The centralizer $C_k$ is connected. The isomorphism of step 2, valid on this fibre by step 7, is $C_k\simeq F_k\times R_k$. Projection to $F_k$ is surjective, since it has the section $f\mapsto(f,1)$. Its continuous image is connected, so $F_k$ is connected. This proves connected geometric fibres without assuming that the original action was inner or faithful.

source.place: Example 2.2.6, pp.66--67; field centralizer connectedness as in Milne, Theorem 17.38.

proof.text: Suppose now $H$ is reductive. Over the fixed algebraically closed field $k$, let $V=R_u(E_k)$ be the smooth connected closed normal unipotent radical provided by [lem-sfb-unipotent-radical-existence]. The projection $V\to R_k$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial], so $V$ factors through the scheme-theoretic kernel $H_k$ of $E_k\to R_k$. It is a smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup of $H_k$: closedness follows from its closed immersion in $E_k$, and normality follows by restricting conjugation from $E_k$. Reductivity of $H_k$ gives $V=1$. Every smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup of $E_k$ is contained in $V$ by the cited radical theorem. Hence $E_k$ is reductive.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.5 proof, p.101: justification that the semidirect product is reductive.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-fixed-subgroup], the centralizer $C_{E_k}(R_k)$ is reductive, since step 10 proved $E_k$ reductive and $R_k$ is an embedded torus. Under $C_k\simeq F_k\times R_k$, the factor $F_k$ is a closed normal subgroup (the kernel of projection to $R_k$). It is smooth by steps 3--6 and smooth base change [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2), and connected by step 9. Thus [lem-sfb-connected-normal-subgroup-reductive] applies and proves $F_k$ reductive. Since this holds for every geometric fibre, the already smooth affine finitely presented group $F$ is reductive by the definition in the item. Rank zero and the trivial action are included: the formulas give $F=H$ and $C=H\times R$ in those cases.

source.place: Paragraph before Remark 3.1.5, p.83, and Corollary 3.3.5 proof, p.101; Milne, Corollaries 17.59 and 21.53.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q158-5950aca36 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read all 11 steps and the statement of every cited node in full. This is a first split, since the imported item had no proof. There are no new nodes and the statement is unchanged. The steps are correct. Steps 1–3: the semidirect product E=H⋊R over an affine base where R=G_m^r; I checked the inverse formula, the closedness of R, and that E is affine, finitely presented and smooth. The centralizer node gives C={(h,t): h fixed}, and C≅F×R. Smoothness of F comes from a lift into C followed by the retraction C→F, so the step never assumes that a closed subgroup of a smooth group is smooth. Steps 4–6: the fixed points form an fpqc sheaf. The fppf splitting cover is refined to a single affine fpqc cover; F descends as an affine scheme, together with its map to H. Closed immersion, affine, lfp and smooth descend by the cited nodes, and the Zariski gluing of the affine pieces works. Step 7 (subgroup property and base change) is elementary, as marked. Steps 8–11 work on geometric fibres. R_k is split by the Nullstellensatz. E_k is connected by the product-components node and a rational point. Torus centralizers in E_k are connected, so F_k is connected. R_u(E_k) maps trivially to R_k, hence lies in H_k and is trivial, so E_k is reductive. C_k is reductive, and F_k, a smooth connected normal subgroup of it, is reductive. I checked this field-level route against the local Milne iAG: Thm 13.1 and Cor 17.57–17.59 use the same G⋊S argument; Thm 17.38 and Cor 14.18 match the inputs to steps 9 and 10. Conrad Ex. 2.2.6 is not available locally (marked WANTED); the relative input it would supply is the existing node lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer. Batch-5: every listed citation (fppf coverings are fpqc, smooth fpqc base descent, the definition of algebraic space, the fibre smoothness criterion, flat tensor injectivity) is a generic scheme or algebra fact.
